One latent process, several observation models

Nicholas J Clark

2026-10-28

Source: vignettes/articles/mvbf.Rmd
mvbf.Rmd

Monitoring programmes often measure one quantity with several methods. A population might be counted along transects, weighed in traps and detected by cameras in the same months. Each method measures the same abundance through an observation process of its own. Fitted separately, each method estimates abundance from its own data alone. Fitted jointly, every method informs one estimate of the shared abundance. Integrated population models combine data sources in this way (Schaub and Abadi 2011).

mvgam fits such a model as a multivariate formula: one bf() per response, each with its own family and covariates. A single trend_formula describes the latent process they share. This article simulates three methods observing one population. We fit the joint model and the three separate models, then compare how closely each recovers the simulated abundance.

The data

The latent abundance ztz_t, on the log scale, follows a stationary AR(1) over 80 months:

zt∼Normal(0.7zt−1,0.4). z_t \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0.7\, z_{t-1},\ 0.4).

Three methods observe it. Transect counts (count) are Poisson with a log link. Survey effort varies by month and enters as an offset. Trap biomass (biomass) is Gamma with a log link and shape 2. A seasonal cycle in month adds to the latent state. Camera detections (camera) are Bernoulli with a logit link. Detection rises by 0.05 on the logit scale with each day the camera is deployed. The cameras run in only 60 of the 80 months.

set.seed(2024)
n_time <- 80
z <- numeric(n_time)
z[1] <- rnorm(1, 0, 0.4 / sqrt(1 - 0.7^2))
for (t in 2:n_time) {
  z[t] <- 0.7 * z[t - 1] + rnorm(1, 0, 0.4)
}

month <- (seq_len(n_time) - 1) %% 12 + 1
log_effort <- log(runif(n_time, 0.8, 1.2))
deploy_days <- runif(n_time, 5, 20)
mu_biomass <- exp(0.5 + sin(2 * pi * month / 12) + z)

mv_data <- data.frame(
  time = seq_len(n_time),
  series = factor("pop1"),
  month = month,
  log_effort = log_effort,
  deploy_days = deploy_days,
  count = rpois(n_time, exp(1.5 + log_effort + z)),
  biomass = rgamma(n_time, shape = 2, rate = 2 / mu_biomass),
  camera = rbinom(n_time, 1, plogis(-0.5 + 0.05 * deploy_days + z))
)
mv_data$camera[-sort(sample.int(n_time, 60))] <- NA
observed <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("count", "biomass", "camera"), function(r) {
  data.frame(time = mv_data$time, value = mv_data[[r]], response = r)
}))
observed$response <- factor(observed$response,
                            levels = c("count", "biomass", "camera"))
ggplot(observed, aes(time, value)) +
  geom_line(data = ~ subset(.x, response != "camera"), colour = "#A25050") +
  geom_point(size = 1, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ response, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Month", y = NULL)

The three simulated monitoring records. The camera record has gaps in the months the cameras did not run.

The joint model

Each response enters through its own bf(), combined with +, carrying its family and its covariates. set_rescor(FALSE) declares that the responses share no residual correlation beyond the latent state. A cyclic smooth of month captures the seasonal cycle in biomass:

joint_formula <-
  bf(count ~ 1 + offset(log_effort), family = poisson()) +
  bf(biomass ~ 1 + s(month, bs = "cc", k = 8), family = Gamma(link = "log")) +
  bf(camera ~ 1 + deploy_days, family = bernoulli()) +
  set_rescor(FALSE)

mod_joint <- mvgam(
  joint_formula,
  trend_formula = ~ AR(p = 1),
  data = mv_data,
  knots = list(month = c(0.5, 12.5)),
  chains = 4, seed = 2024, silent = 2
)

The latent state ztz_t enters the linear predictor of every response. Because a response with no record drops out of the likelihood, a month without a camera record informs the state through the count and biomass likelihoods alone.

Checking each response

pp_check() compares draws from the posterior predictive distribution with the data. Without resp it draws one panel per response:

pp_check(mod_joint, ndraws = 50)

Posterior predictive checks for each response. A rootogram compares the frequency of each count. A density overlay checks the biomass record. Bars give the share of each camera outcome.

conditional_effects() draws each response’s covariate effects on that response’s scale, with the latent process held out. The simulated biomass cycle peaks in month 3:

ce <- conditional_effects(mod_joint)
wrap_plots(plot(ce, plot = FALSE), ncol = 2)

Expected biomass by month and camera detection probability by deployment days, with 95% credible intervals.

The fitted biomass curve peaks in month 10. The deployment slope is 0.08 [-0.04, 0.21] on the logit scale, against the 0.05 used to simulate the data.

What the joint model gains

To compare, we fit each method on its own, with the same AR(1) state:

fit_one <- function(formula, family) {
  mvgam(formula, trend_formula = ~ AR(p = 1), family = family,
        data = mv_data, knots = list(month = c(0.5, 12.5)),
        chains = 4, seed = 2024, silent = 2)
}
mod_count <- fit_one(count ~ 1 + offset(log_effort), poisson())
mod_biomass <- fit_one(biomass ~ 1 + s(month, bs = "cc", k = 8),
                       Gamma(link = "log"))
mod_camera <- fit_one(camera ~ 1 + deploy_days, bernoulli())

hindcast(type = "trend") returns each model’s posterior for the latent state:

fits <- list(
  "Joint" = mod_joint,
  "Counts alone" = mod_count,
  "Biomass alone" = mod_biomass,
  "Camera alone" = mod_camera
)
truth <- data.frame(time = seq_len(n_time), z = z)
wrap_plots(lapply(names(fits), function(nm) {
  plot(hindcast(fits[[nm]], type = "trend")) +
    geom_point(aes(time, z), data = truth, shape = 4, size = 1) +
    labs(title = nm, y = "Latent state")
}), ncol = 2)

Posterior medians and 95% credible intervals of the latent state from the joint model and from each method alone. Crosses mark the simulated state. 

recovery <- t(vapply(fits, function(fit) {
  s <- summary(hindcast(fit, type = "trend"))
  c(RMSE = sqrt(mean((s$predQ50 - z)^2)),
    `Interval width` = mean(s$predQ97.5 - s$predQ2.5))
}, numeric(2)))
round(recovery, 2)
#>               RMSE Interval width
#> Joint         0.26           1.24
#> Counts alone  0.32           1.36
#> Biomass alone 0.47           1.74
#> Camera alone  0.57           3.99

Ordered by root mean squared error against the simulated state, the fits rank joint (0.26), counts alone (0.32), biomass alone (0.47), and camera alone (0.57). Intervals are narrowest in the joint fit and widest in the camera alone fit. A single binary record per month constrains abundance weakly.

Forecasts

forecast() extends the latent state past the last month and passes it through each response’s observation model. The new data hold unit survey effort, the calendar month of each future time point and 15 deployment days for the camera. type = "expected" returns the expected count, the expected biomass and the detection probability:

newdata <- data.frame(
  time = n_time + 1:6,
  series = factor("pop1"),
  month = (n_time + 0:5) %% 12 + 1,
  log_effort = 0,
  deploy_days = 15,
  count = NA, biomass = NA, camera = NA
)
fc <- forecast(mod_joint, newdata = newdata, type = "expected")
plot(fc)

Expected values for each response over the training months and a six-month forecast. Points are the observations.

The forecast object also feeds score() once the held-out observations arrive.

Against the simulated abundance, the four fits ranked joint (0.26), counts alone (0.32), biomass alone (0.47), and camera alone (0.57) by error. A single binary outcome per month constrains the state weakly. Fitted jointly, the camera record takes the state the other methods estimate. A monitoring programme that measures one population by several methods can fit them to one latent process and let each method inform the rest.
